source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompts copying clinician reasoning modes (differential diagnosis, intuitive, analytic, Bayesian) were compared with plain chain of thought on open-ended MedQA. The intuitive (recognition-style) prompt was the only mode that never hurt either model.
numbers: Test set 518 USMLE Step 2/3 questions (497 usable for GPT-4). GPT-3.5: CoT 46%, intuitive 48% (+1.7, P=0.9), analytic 40% (-6, P=0.001), differential 38% (-8, P<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4, P=0.02). GPT-4: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78%, analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4, P=0.07). Each prompt had two worked examples.
quote: significantly worse with differential diagnosis, analytical, and Bayesian inference CoT prompts
limits: No accuracy gain from any reasoning prompt for GPT-4 (all inside CIs). 2023 models. MedQA stems, not real notes. Two raters, kappa 0.93 and 0.98.
agent_relevance: Telling a strong model to follow an analytic or differential routine gave no gain; a weak model lost accuracy. Imposed structure must earn its place, so no default reasoning ritual (supports G1).

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview was tested on NEJM clinicopathologic cases, R-IDEA documentation of reasoning, management cases, probabilistic reasoning and real emergency-department cases, against hundreds of physicians.
numbers: NEJM CPC (143 cases): correct diagnosis in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7-84.8), first diagnosis correct 52%. On 70 cases earlier used for GPT-4: exact or very close 88.6% vs 72.9%. R-IDEA perfect score 78/80 vs GPT-4 47/80, attendings 28/80, residents 16/80. Management cases median 86% vs GPT-4 42%, physicians+GPT-4 41%, physicians 34%. Real ED cases (Bond 4-5): o1 65.8% triage, 69.6% ED physician, 79.7% ICU vs physician 1 at 54.4/60.8/75.9%.
limits: Text only; historical controls for some arms; CPC cases may overlap training data (no pre/post cutoff difference: 79.8% vs 73.5%, p=0.59). Not about illness scripts directly.
agent_relevance: Strong models already match or beat physicians on the output of recognition plus reasoning, so the bottleneck is not stored knowledge but how it is used under uncertainty and cost.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench, MAI-DxO)
finding: A scaffold of five roles (hypothesis tracker, test chooser, challenger, cost steward, checklist) on one model raised accuracy on stepwise NEJM CPC cases. The hypothesis role keeps a ranked differential with Bayesian-style updates, a direct class-library plus update loop.
numbers: 304 NEJM CPC cases. Physicians (median 12 years) 20% at $2,963/case. GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745; o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO on o3: 79.9% at $2,397; no-budget 81.9%; ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. Gains significant for all models (p<0.005) except o3 and o4-mini on accuracy (their cost cuts were significant). Held-out 56-case test set kept the relative gains.
quote: off-the-shelf o3 seemed to anchor on initial impressions
limits: Gatekeeper is a language model that can invent test results; physicians barred from outside resources; MAI-DxO tuned on GPT-4.1 and a validation set. Vendor study, not independent.
agent_relevance: Gains were largest for weaker models. Manual inspection: plain o3 anchored on first impressions; the challenger role and explicit hypothesis tracking made it seek disconfirming evidence. Matches our S2 represent plus doubt-on-signal design, but the panel is five roles of one model (G4: not independent).

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Seven clinically common cognitive biases were injected into USMLE questions (including self-diagnosis, false consensus, frequency, recency, status quo, confirmation). Accuracy dropped for every model; GPT-4 was most robust.
numbers: 1,273 USMLE Step 1-3 questions, 6 LLMs. GPT-4 worst drop 14.0% (false consensus), only 0.2% for confirmation; GPT-3.5 average drop 37.4%. Averaged over models: false consensus -24.9%, frequency -18.2%, recency -12.9%, confirmation -8.1%. Bias-education prompt lifted GPT-4 frequency-bias accuracy 0.627 to 0.720; one-shot raised recency 0.679 to 0.742. Mitigated accuracy never reached the no-bias level.
limits: Multiple choice, single-letter answers; bias statements are crude. Safety filters blocked 94-99% of one/few-shot queries for one PaLM model, so it was excluded from those arms.
agent_relevance: A recognizer that matches stored classes is pulled by the frame of the question. A warning plus a worked bad example helps a little but does not remove it, so frame checks should be done in code, not by a warning line.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
finding: On 2,400 real MIMIC-IV patients with four abdominal diseases, open models diagnosed worse than doctors, skipped guideline tests, and were sensitive to how much and in what order information appeared.
numbers: Doctors beat models by 16-25 points (hospitalists 87.5% resident, 92.5% senior). With self-directed information gathering, mean accuracy fell: Llama 2 Chat 45.5% vs 58.8% with full information; OASST 54.9% vs 67.8%; WizardLM 53.9% vs 65.1%. Fewer exams helped: cholecystitis +18.5% (Chat) with only the radiology report. Order of information changed accuracy by up to 18.0% (Chat, pancreatitis).
limits: Older open models (Llama 2 era), four abdominal diseases; no GPT-4-class model. Specialist medical models were no better.
agent_relevance: Model recognition degrades with more evidence and with ordering, unlike an expert whose script filters cues. Supports a program-side cue selector and fixed information order rather than dumping all data.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 did not raise their diagnostic reasoning score, but GPT-4 alone scored higher than both physician groups.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), up to 6 vignettes, 60 min. Median score 76% LLM group vs 74% conventional, adjusted +2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, P=.60). Time per case 519 s vs 565 s (P=.20). LLM alone +16 points over conventional (95% CI 2-30, P=.03). 244 cases completed.
limits: Zero-shot prompt only; physicians often did not use the model well; small N; vignettes from a classic computer-diagnosis study.
agent_relevance: Access to model output is not the same as using it. The agent must make class-library recall a forced step, not an optional lookup.

source: Human-AI collaboration in clinical reasoning: a UK replication and interaction analysis (Diagnosis, 2026)
finding: Replicates Goh et al. in UK physicians. Here LLM access did help physicians, but they still scored far below the LLM alone because they asked it only about a third of the questions.
numbers: 22 physicians, 4 vignettes, 2 with LLM. With LLM 74.3% vs 65.7% without (p=0.001). LLM alone above physician+LLM by 21.3 points (p<0.001). Only 30% of case questions were posed to the LLM; SD of improvement 12.8%.
limits: Abstract only (PubMed record read). Small within-subject study.
agent_relevance: The main effect differs from the US null result; the shared finding is the under-use gap. Design the agent so the model is always consulted.

source: McDuff et al. (2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models (AMIE)
finding: A model tuned for diagnostic reasoning produced better differentials than unaided clinicians and raised clinicians' own lists when used as an aid.
numbers: 302 NEJM case reports, 20 clinicians. AMIE alone top-1 29.2%, top-10 59.1%; unaided clinicians top-1 15.9%, top-10 33.6%; after search aid 24.3%/44.5%; after AMIE aid 25.2%/51.8%. 56-case no-overlap set: AMIE top-10 55.4%.
limits: Published case reports may be in training data; clinicians were not the raters used for earlier GPT-4 work; no real-time pressure.
agent_relevance: Breadth (top-10) is much higher than top-1. Recalling many candidate classes is cheap for a model; ranking them is the hard part, so ranking stays in code (G5).

source: Cabral et al. (2024) Clinical reasoning of a generative AI model compared with physicians (R-IDEA)
finding: GPT-4 reasoning documentation was scored with R-IDEA against attendings and residents. Numbers here come from Brodeur et al. 2024, which re-reports them.
numbers: R-IDEA perfect score 47/80 GPT-4, 28/80 attendings, 16/80 residents (as quoted in Brodeur 2024, which I opened).
limits: The PMC page was blocked by a captcha this session and the PubMed abstract has no results. Any claim of more incorrect reasoning in GPT-4 text was not verified.
agent_relevance: A model can write good-looking reasoning while some of it is wrong; rationale needs code-level checks.

source: Strong et al. (2023) Chatbot vs medical student performance on free-response clinical reasoning examinations (JAMA Intern Med)
finding: Compares GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with first- and second-year medical students on free-response clinical reasoning exams.
numbers: Not verified: the abstract has no figures and the full text was blocked.
limits: Research letter; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Early marker that free-response recognition items are in reach of chatbots; no design use beyond that.

source: Script concordance benchmark: Assessment of Large Language Models in Clinical Reasoning (NEJM AI, 2025)
finding: The largest SCT benchmark for LLMs. Models score lower on SCT than on multiple choice, and reasoning-tuned models are over-confident: they use extreme ratings (+2/-2) and rarely 0.
numbers: 750 SCT items from 10 datasets (9 new). Ten LLMs vs 1,070 students, 193 residents, 300 attendings. o3 67.8% +-1.2, GPT-4o 63.9% +-1.3, o1-preview 58.2% +-1.3, DeepSeek R1 55.5% +-1.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro 52.1% +-1.4. Models matched or beat students but did not reach senior residents or attendings.
limits: Abstract only. SCT is scored against an expert-panel majority, so panel bias enters.
agent_relevance: SCT directly tests whether new evidence moves a hypothesis the way a script predicts. The extreme-rating habit shows reasoning models over-commit when evidence is mixed; argues for a program-side uncertainty scale and G1.

source: Evaluating how different versions of ChatGPT align with expert opinions on geriatric script concordance tests (Eur Geriatr Med, 2026)
finding: Four ChatGPT versions answered 20 geriatric SCT items and were scored against 43 experts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 8/20 (agreed with the expert majority on 15% of answers); GPT-4 15.6/20 and GPT-5 15.2/20 (45% agreement); GPT-4o 13.6/20.
limits: Abstract only; 20 items, one specialty; the newer 4o scored below 4.
agent_relevance: Version-to-version noise is large on small SCTs; any SCT-based check in our loop needs many items and repeated runs.

source: Evaluating the clinical reasoning of generative AI in palliative care: a comparison with five years of pharmacy learners (J Palliat Med, 2025)
finding: Four commercial LLMs took a 16-item SCT that pharmacy students took in 2018-2023.
numbers: LLM mean score 0.43 vs students 0.47 (p=0.55). Best model GPT-4.0 at 0.57.
limits: Abstract only; very few items; LLMs were prompted past default safety refusals.
agent_relevance: In a niche, value-laden domain LLMs fall to student level on script-style judgments.

source: Introducing AI as members of script concordance test expert reference panel (Med Teach, 2025)
finding: ChatGPT-4 and o1-preview served as simulated expert reference panels for an ophthalmology SCT, against a 15-person human panel.
numbers: Human experts scored highest on most vignettes; o1 mean scores were closer to experts than GPT-4 scores. Exact means not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; one clerkship.
agent_relevance: A simulated panel drawn from one model is a set of correlated voters (G4); use it to draft items, not as ground truth.

source: Teaching clinical reasoning using AI-generated script concordance tests: mixed methods formative evaluation (JMIR Form Res, 2025)
finding: ChatGPT-4o wrote a 32-item SCT; six LLMs acted as simulated experts. Models given course documents agreed more with students than the same models without them.
numbers: 25 second-year students; mean score 22.8/32 (SD 1.6); Cronbach alpha 0.76. Trained-AI concordance with students rho=0.64 vs untrained rho=0.41. AI feedback picked as most helpful in 62.5% of items.
limits: Context loading only, no fine-tuning. Concordance is with students, not experts. One school, cardiology and respirology.
agent_relevance: Putting course material in context moved model judgments toward the target group: a class library in the prompt shifts script-style answers.

source: Using ChatGPT in psychiatry to design script concordance tests in undergraduate medical education (JMIR Med Educ, 2024)
finding: 102 raters could not tell ChatGPT-made SCTs from expert-made ones, but the AI scenarios were caricatured and simple.
numbers: 3 ChatGPT vs 3 expert SCTs: scenario P=.84, questions P=.99, expert opinion P=.07.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Model-written cases are prototypical. Treat model-written exemplars as prototypes, not as the awkward atypical cases that break scripts.

source: Large language models for generating script concordance test in obstetrics and gynecology: ChatGPT and Claude (Med Teach, 2025)
finding: ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet made SCT items judged by 16 panelists on 11 criteria.
numbers: Criteria met overall: 90.57% (GPT-4o), 91.48% (Claude 3.5). Weakest criterion, right difficulty for students: 71.25% and 76.25%.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Models write textbook-typical items well; difficulty calibration is their weak point.

source: Expert assessment of ChatGPT's ability to generate illness scripts: an evaluative study (BMC Med Educ, 2024)
finding: GPT-4 wrote complete illness scripts (pathophysiology, epidemiology, time course, signs and symptoms, diagnosis, treatment) for 184 Japanese-curriculum diseases; three physicians graded them.
numbers: A (sufficient) 103/184 = 56.0%; B (partly lacking) 52 = 28.3%; C (deficient) 29 = 15.8%. Cardiovascular and psychiatric scripts had more C ratings. Example errors: varicella given droplet transmission; family history omitted for genetic disease. Prompt held three example scripts and a 20-30 word cap per item.
limits: GPT-4 of 25 July 2023; Japanese curriculum; three physicians whose own scripts differ; no test of whether scripts improved diagnosis.
agent_relevance: About 16% of generated class entries are deficient and 44% are not fully adequate, so an LLM-built class library needs a source or code check before use.

source: Leveraging artificial intelligence to accelerate competency development in diagnostic reasoning of medical students (Med Teach, 2026)
finding: Randomized trial: a Copilot chatbot giving instruction and feedback on illness script writing beat conventional teaching on script quality.
numbers: 83 students; Illness Script Assessment Tool: structure OR 3.7, content OR 3.3, maturity OR 2.9 at immediate post; composite OR 3.2 (T2) and 2.7 (T3, new cases).
limits: Abstract only; script quality is a rated proxy, not diagnostic accuracy; one school.
agent_relevance: Structured script feedback is learnable and checkable for humans; suggests an explicit script form (enabling conditions, fault, consequences) can be a checkable slot structure.

source: AI teaches surgical diagnostic reasoning to medical students (J Surg Educ, 2025)
finding: A fully automated AI system wrote MCQs and feedback on five abdominal-pain diagnoses; Year-1 students beat a Year-2 control.
numbers: 38 intervention vs 33 control; better at once and at 2 weeks (both p<0.001); 0.6% of feedback statements had minor issues; AI cost $0.51 total.
limits: Non-randomized; control in a different year; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Contrasting a few similar diseases is cheap to generate with an LLM and reviewable.

source: Test-retest reliability of LLMs and their concordance with human experts in rubric-based scoring of clinical summary statements (JMIR Med Educ, 2026)
finding: LLMs scored students' one-line problem representations on semantic qualifiers, transformation, narrowing and global quality. Binary items agreed better than abstract ternary ones, and prompting mattered a lot.
numbers: 122 statements (English and German), 6 virtual cases, 4 LLMs x 5 runs x 4 prompt types. Large models ICC>=0.92; Claude ICC and Fleiss kappa >=0.99. Mistral Large: global AC2=0.921, narrowing 0.842, semantic qualifiers 0.820. GPT-4o zero-shot semantic qualifiers AC2=0.257 while factual accuracy peaked at AC1=0.880 with few-shot CoT. Mistral 7B: semantic qualifiers AC2=0.876 but 'person' AC1=0.037.
limits: No single model-prompt pair was best on every component; two expert raters; small open model unstable.
agent_relevance: Semantic qualifiers (abstract paired terms such as acute versus chronic) are what script theory says experts use. Models judge them reliably only with the right prompt, so any rubric grader must be tested per component.

source: Chen et al. (2024) CoD, Towards an Interpretable Medical Agent using Chain of Diagnosis (DiagnosisGPT)
finding: Splits diagnosis into a chain: abstract the symptoms, retrieve candidate diseases, analyse, then output a confidence distribution over diseases; the entropy drop picks the next question to ask.
numbers: Trained on 48,020 synthetic cases built from disease encyclopedias; covers 9,604 diseases. The paper reports DiagnosisGPT ahead of other LLMs on automatic diagnosis benchmarks (exact scores not copied here).
limits: Training cases are synthetic text from encyclopedias, so they mirror textbook prototypes, not messy records. Fine-tuned, not prompt-only. Benchmark scores not read in detail.
agent_relevance: A direct use of class retrieval, a distribution over classes, and information gain in an agent loop. A confidence distribution can be normalized in code (G5).

source: Gao et al. (2025) Leveraging medical knowledge graphs into large language models for diagnosis prediction (DR.KNOWS)
finding: Retrieves paths from the UMLS knowledge graph (up to 2 hops from concepts in the note), ranks them, and feeds them to a text model that predicts diagnoses.
numbers: Two EHR sets: MIMIC-III (ICU) and an in-house hospital set. T5 with DR.KNOWS paths had the highest ROUGE-L and concept-F1; human raters judged rationales as aligned with correct clinical reasoning. Specific F1 values not copied.
limits: Only part of the paper read (abstract, setup, datasets). Authors flag KG bias and concept-extraction errors upstream.
agent_relevance: A knowledge graph is a structured stand-in for category knowledge; retrieved paths act like script slots. A template for a retrieval step before represent.

source: Structured reasoning failures compromise LLM interpretation of clinical oncology notes (npj Digit Med, 2026)
finding: GPT-4 errors on oncology notes were mostly cognitive-bias patterns (confirmation, anchoring, omission); GPT-5.1 cut but did not remove them; LLM judges detected errors but could not classify them.
numbers: GPT-4 reasoning errors in 23.1% of note interpretations, two cohorts, three cancers. Self-mitigation gave only modest improvement.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Human-like bias patterns appear in model output, and model critics cannot sort them (G5: use code or external checks).

source: Mitigating cognitive biases in clinical decision-making through multi-agent conversations using large language models (JMIR, 2024)
finding: GPT-4 role agents (two junior residents with one as devil's advocate, a senior doctor or expert, a recorder) revisited misdiagnosis cases taken from the bias literature.
numbers: 16 bias-driven misdiagnosis case reports, 5 repeats, 240 responses. First-responder initial diagnosis 0/80 correct. Final top-2 accuracy: framework 3: 51/80 (64%), framework 4: 55/80 (69%), framework 4-C: 61/80 (76%, OR 3.49 vs humans, P=.002). Humans: initial 13/48 (27%), final 23/48 (48%). Correct in 13/16 scenarios.
limits: Cases were chosen because they fooled humans; model scored on top-2 while humans gave a top diagnosis plus 2 others; same model plays all roles; no real patients.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as MAI-DxO: a challenger role fixes anchoring. The correlated-voters caution (G4) still applies, so trigger the challenger on a code signal.

source: Miller, Pople and Myers (1982) INTERNIST-1, an experimental computer-based diagnostic consultant
finding: Older AI system that matched findings to a stored library of disease profiles with frequency and evoking-strength weights, then used the leading candidates to choose questions. An ancestor of a class library.
numbers: Not verified this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; only the PubMed title record was seen. Limits known from the literature (not verified here): weak with several simultaneous disorders, no learning.
agent_relevance: The weighted disease-profile library is a machine form of illness scripts; evoke, then discriminate, is the loop that MAI-DxO and CoD re-create with LLMs.

source: Clinical reasoning and artificial intelligence: can AI really think? (Trans Am Clin Climatol Assoc, 2024)
finding: Commentary: LLMs are largely pattern recognition; compares hypothetico-deductive reasoning with illness scripts against inductive mechanism-based reasoning and warns about bias and adaptive expertise.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Opinion piece; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Frames the gap we care about: recognition from stored classes versus mechanism reasoning when no class fits; the agent needs a route for the no-match case.

source: Effect of large language model on diagnostic accuracy and clinical completeness among nephrology fellows managing transplant infection (Int Urol Nephrol, 2026)
finding: Fellows given GPT-4o exemplar answers improved on transplant infection vignettes, mostly where knowledge is a stored protocol, and not in dual-infection cases.
numbers: 12 fellows, 30 vignettes, 1,200 responses. Median accuracy 72% to 85.5% (+13.0, p<0.001), completeness 1.9 to 2.5, time 7.1 to 5.9 min; fungal +19.2, viral +17.5; one clinically significant hallucination (3.3%); little help in dual-infection scenarios.
limits: Abstract only; single center, pre-post, no randomization.
agent_relevance: Help is weakest where two classes combine (dual infection), the boundary of single-script recognition.
